title: Urinary Biochemistry and Nutrition
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the kidney as a metabolic organ: how it reclaims glucose and filtered proteins, activates vitamin D, sets the distribution of potassium, senses oxygen to make erythropoietin, and is injured by the metabolites of ethylene glycol and by the lipid changes of nephrotic syndrome. Board questions in this area usually hand you a lab panel, a urinalysis, or an ECG and ask you to predict the next value or name the failed step. If you can trace each abnormal value back to a transporter, an enzyme, or a feedback loop, you can work out patterns you have never memorized.
prerequisites: Glomerular filtration, filtered load, and proximal tubule transport (UR-6)
Secondary active transport driven by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
Resting membrane potential and the Nernst equation for K+
Anion gap and the classification of metabolic acidosis (UR-7)
Lipoprotein classes and the LDL receptor pathway

connections.how: Potassium sets the resting potential and repolarization of cardiac cells, so its disorders appear as predictable changes in T waves, the QRS, and U waves.
Diabetic glucosuria and the parathyroid and vitamin D disorders are endocrine diseases whose laboratory signature is written by renal transport.
Damage to the filtration barrier explains glomerular proteinuria, the hyperlipidemia of nephrotic syndrome, and lipiduria.
Erythropoietin from the kidney is the main hormonal signal that sets red cell production in the marrow.
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma loses VHL function and can secrete erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythemia.

terms.def: The amount of a solute filtered per minute, equal to GFR multiplied by its plasma concentration (for freely filtered solutes).
The highest rate at which a saturable carrier system can reabsorb a solute; for glucose about 375 mg/min in an adult.
The plasma concentration at which a solute first appears in the urine; for glucose about 200 mg/dL.
The rounded portion of the titration curve between threshold and Tm, caused by nephrons saturating at different plasma levels.
Increased urine flow caused by an unreabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubular lumen.
Free immunoglobulin light chains in the urine, produced in excess by a plasma cell clone.
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the active hormone formed by 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the proximal tubule.
A phosphaturic hormone from osteocytes that lowers proximal phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
The distribution of potassium between intracellular and extracellular fluid, as distinct from external balance between intake and excretion.
A transcription factor degraded in normal oxygen and stabilized in hypoxia, where it switches on the erythropoietin gene.
Measured serum osmolality minus calculated osmolality; a gap above about 10 mOsm/kg signals an unmeasured osmole such as a toxic alcohol.
A degenerated tubular epithelial cell or macrophage filled with lipid droplets, shed into the urine in heavy proteinuria.

sections.title: Glucose reabsorption, the renal threshold, and osmotic diuresis

blocks.text: Glucose is small and uncharged, so it is freely filtered, and its filtered load equals GFR times plasma glucose. At a GFR of 125 mL/min and a plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL (1 mg/mL), about 125 mg is filtered each minute, and normally all of it is reclaimed in the proximal tubule, leaving urine essentially glucose free.

Reabsorption is secondary active transport. The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase keeps intracellular Na+ low and the cell interior negative, and apical sodium-glucose cotransporters use that gradient to move glucose uphill into the cell. SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule (S1 and S2 segments) is a high capacity, low affinity carrier with a 1 Na+ to 1 glucose ratio and reclaims about 90% of filtered glucose. SGLT1 in the late proximal tubule (S3) is a low capacity, high affinity carrier with a 2 Na+ to 1 glucose ratio that scavenges the remainder. Glucose then leaves the cell down its gradient by facilitated diffusion through basolateral GLUT2 (GLUT1 in S3).
Saturation, threshold, and splay

Because the number of carriers is fixed, reabsorption rises with filtered load only until the carriers saturate. The whole-kidney transport maximum is about 375 mg/min. Glucose nevertheless appears in urine at a plasma level of about 200 mg/dL, when the filtered load (about 250 mg/min) is still below Tm, because nephrons differ in glomerular size and carrier density; those with high filtered load relative to their carriers saturate first. This gap between threshold and full saturation is splay. Above Tm, every additional milligram filtered is excreted, so excretion rises linearly with plasma glucose.

blocks.title: How much glucose reaches the urine
blocks.text: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes has a plasma glucose of 400 mg/dL (4 mg/mL) and a GFR of 125 mL/min. Filtered load is 4 mg/mL times 125 mL/min, or 500 mg/min. The tubules can reabsorb at most about 375 mg/min, so about 125 mg/min is excreted, roughly 180 g/day if sustained. At 150 mg/dL the filtered load is only 188 mg/min, below threshold for nearly all nephrons, so the dipstick (glucose oxidase) is negative. Between about 200 mg/dL and the level at which filtered load reaches Tm (about 300 mg/dL), simple subtraction predicts no excretion, yet some glucose appears because low-capacity nephrons saturate early (splay).

blocks.title: From hyperglycemia to volume depletion
steps: Plasma glucose rises above about 200 mg/dL
Filtered load exceeds carrier capacity in some nephrons
Unreabsorbed glucose stays in the tubular lumen as an osmole
Luminal osmoles hold water; luminal Na+ is diluted
Less water and Na+ are reabsorbed downstream
Polyuria, thirst, and extracellular volume depletion
blocks.caption: Glucosuria drives an osmotic diuresis that loses water in excess of sodium, so volume depletion and rising plasma osmolality follow.

blocks.text: Osmotic diuresis explains the classic triad of diabetes: polyuria, polydipsia, and, with ongoing calorie loss as urinary glucose, weight loss. Water is lost in excess of sodium, so plasma osmolality rises and the falling GFR of volume depletion further raises plasma glucose, a cycle that underlies the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.

Glucosuria with a normal plasma glucose means the transport system, not the filtered load, has changed. Causes include generalized proximal tubule dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome, with glucose, amino acids, phosphate, and bicarbonate wasted together), isolated familial renal glucosuria from SLC5A2 (SGLT2) mutations, and pregnancy, in which a higher GFR raises filtered load and the threshold falls. Pharmacologic SGLT2 inhibition confirms the model: blocking the early carrier produces glucosuria and a mild osmotic natriuresis at normal plasma glucose.

Normal urine contains less than about 150 mg of protein per day, of which less than 30 mg is albumin. Two systems keep it that low. The glomerular filtration barrier (fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane with its negatively charged heparan sulfate, and the podocyte slit diaphragm built on nephrin) restricts molecules by size and charge. Albumin (about 69 kDa, anionic) is large enough and negative enough to be held back almost completely. Smaller proteins, such as beta-2 microglobulin (about 12 kDa), free light chains (about 22 kDa as monomers), lysozyme, and retinol-binding protein, pass the filter and are reclaimed by the proximal tubule, where the megalin and cubilin receptors bind them for endocytosis and lysosomal breakdown to amino acids.

Each type of proteinuria breaks one step of this system. In glomerular proteinuria the barrier is damaged, so albumin crosses in large amounts; loss of charge selectivity alone (as in minimal change disease) leaks mainly albumin (selective proteinuria), while structural damage leaks larger proteins such as IgG as well (nonselective). Excretion often exceeds 3.5 g/day, the nephrotic range. In overflow proteinuria the barrier and tubule are normal but plasma carries so much of a small protein that the filtered load exceeds the proximal reabsorptive capacity, which is limited like that of glucose. The classic example is Bence Jones light chains from a plasma cell clone in multiple myeloma; myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobin in intravascular hemolysis behave the same way. In tubular proteinuria the filter and plasma are normal, but injured proximal cells fail to reclaim the small proteins filtered every day, so beta-2 microglobulin and retinol-binding protein appear, usually in amounts below about 2 g/day.

blocks.title: Three mechanisms of proteinuria
rows: Free light chains, myoglobin, or hemoglobin
Often weak or negative for light chains
Diabetic nephropathy, minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy
Fanconi syndrome, heavy metal or drug injury, interstitial nephritis
blocks.caption: Locate the failed step first; the protein type and the dipstick result follow from it.

blocks.text: The urine dipstick uses a pH indicator dye that changes color when protein binds it, and it reacts mainly with albumin. A negative or weak dipstick with a high measured total urine protein (by sulfosalicylic acid precipitation or a quantitative protein to creatinine ratio) therefore points to light chains or tubular proteins, and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation identifies a monoclonal light chain.

The categories interact. Light chains overloading the proximal tubule are directly toxic to it and can cause an acquired Fanconi syndrome, adding tubular proteinuria, and in the distal nephron they bind uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) to form obstructing casts (myeloma cast nephropathy). Heavy glomerular proteinuria also overwhelms and injures proximal cells, so most glomerular diseases carry some tubular damage.

sections.title: Vitamin D activation and calcium, phosphate, and PTH patterns

blocks.text: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) forms in skin when ultraviolet B light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol; D3 and plant-derived D2 are also absorbed from the diet. The liver adds a 25-hydroxyl group to form 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol), the main circulating and storage form and the best measure of vitamin D status because its production is largely unregulated. The regulated step is in mitochondria of proximal tubule cells, where 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) forms 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol).

1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH and by low phosphate, and suppressed by FGF23, high phosphate, and calcitriol itself, which also induces 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) to inactivate it. PTH, acting through its Gs-coupled receptor, raises plasma calcium by three routes: bone resorption (indirectly, through RANKL from osteoblasts), increased calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, and calcitriol synthesis. At the same time it removes NaPi-IIa cotransporters from the proximal tubule brush border, causing phosphaturia, so the phosphate released from bone does not accumulate. Calcitriol increases intestinal absorption of both calcium and phosphate and suppresses PTH gene transcription.

blocks.title: Calcium, PTH, and calcitriol feedback
steps: Plasma ionized calcium falls
Calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells signals less
PTH secretion rises
Proximal tubule 1-alpha-hydroxylase makes more calcitriol
Gut calcium absorption, bone release, and distal reabsorption rise
Plasma calcium returns toward normal and PTH falls
blocks.caption: Negative feedback through the calcium-sensing receptor; PTH-driven phosphaturia keeps phosphate from rising.

blocks.text: In chronic kidney disease, a falling GFR retains phosphate. FGF23 rises early to excrete it and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and loss of proximal tubule mass removes the enzyme itself, so calcitriol falls. Less calcitriol means less intestinal calcium, phosphate binds ionized calcium, and the parathyroid glands, now lacking calcitriol suppression, enlarge and secrete more PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), leading to renal osteodystrophy. In primary hyperparathyroidism, usually a single adenoma, PTH is autonomous: calcium is high, phosphate is low from phosphaturia, and calcitriol is high. In vitamin D deficiency, low calcium absorption drives PTH up; PTH restores calcium toward normal at the cost of phosphaturia, so phosphate is low.

blocks.title: Mineral patterns (normal total calcium about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL, phosphate about 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL)
rows: 25-hydroxyvitamin D low; calcitriol may be normal
blocks.caption: Phosphate separates the two secondary forms: high in CKD (failed excretion) and low in vitamin D deficiency (PTH phosphaturia).

blocks.text: Hypomagnesemia, usually below about 1 mg/dL (normal about 1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL), causes hypocalcemia that does not correct with calcium alone. Low intracellular magnesium enhances signaling by the calcium-sensing receptor, so PTH release is suppressed as if calcium were high, and magnesium-dependent adenylyl cyclase in bone and kidney responds poorly to the PTH that is released. PTH is therefore inappropriately low for the calcium, and calcitriol falls with it. The same deficiency causes renal potassium wasting, so hypokalemia often travels with it.

blocks.predict: A patient has calcium 7.2 mg/dL, low magnesium, and a PTH in the normal range. Is the parathyroid response normal?
blocks.explain: No. Hypocalcemia should raise PTH well above normal. A normal value is inappropriately low because magnesium deficiency impairs PTH release and action, and calcium will stay low until magnesium is restored.
blocks.check: The paragraph on hypomagnesemia and the last row of the mineral patterns table.

blocks.text: About 98% of body potassium is intracellular (about 140 mEq/L in cells versus 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L in plasma), and the gradient is maintained by the Na+/K+-ATPase. A potassium load is first moved into cells (internal balance) and then excreted over hours (external balance, mainly by principal cells under aldosterone). A small shift across cell membranes therefore changes the serum value a great deal, without any change in total body potassium.

blocks.title: Shifts of potassium across cell membranes
rows: Stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase (and Na+/H+ exchange, which supplies Na+ for the pump)
Gs and cAMP increase Na+/K+-ATPase activity
H+ leaves cells to buffer the ECF; K+ enters to preserve electroneutrality
H+ enters cells to be buffered; K+ leaves
Rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, hemolysis, or crush injury release cell contents
Loss of tonic pump stimulation, as in diabetic ketoacidosis
Water leaves cells, concentrating intracellular K+ and carrying it out by solvent drag
blocks.caption: These shifts change serum K+ without changing total body K+.

blocks.text: Two refinements matter on exams. First, mineral (non-anion gap) acidosis shifts potassium far more than organic acidosis, because lactate and ketoanions can enter cells with H+, so less K+ must leave. Second, diabetic ketoacidosis shows how shifts can hide depletion: insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality raise serum K+ even though osmotic diuresis has depleted total body potassium, so serum K+ falls sharply once insulin drives it back into cells. A falsely high value (pseudohyperkalemia) comes from hemolysis in the sample tube or from potassium released by very high platelet or white cell counts during clotting.
Why the ECG changes

The resting membrane potential of cardiac cells lies near the K+ equilibrium potential, which depends on the ratio of intracellular to extracellular K+. In hyperkalemia this ratio falls, so the resting potential becomes less negative. Partial depolarization inactivates some fast Na+ channels, slowing phase 0 and conduction. At the same time, high extracellular K+ increases the conductance of the delayed rectifier K+ channels, so repolarization is faster. Faster repolarization appears first as peaked T waves; slowing conduction then produces the later changes in the table below. Skeletal muscle shows the same partial depolarization as weakness.

In hypokalemia the resting potential becomes more negative, but K+ conductance falls, so repolarization is delayed. The T wave flattens and a U wave (a small deflection after the T wave, best seen in V2 and V3) becomes prominent. Delayed repolarization and increased automaticity favor early afterdepolarizations and ectopic beats, and the risk is greater when Na+/K+-ATPase is also inhibited, as by digoxin. Skeletal muscle weakness, cramps, and ileus follow from hyperpolarization, which moves the resting potential further from threshold.

blocks.caption: Normal ECG for reference against the potassium changes described above.

blocks.title: ECG findings in order of severity
rows: Peaked, narrow T waves; shortened QT
Flat or absent P waves, long PR, wide QRS, sine wave, ventricular fibrillation or asystole
Prominent U waves, long QU interval, ectopy, torsades de pointes
blocks.caption: ECG changes correlate only loosely with the serum value; the rate of change matters as well.

blocks.predict: A patient with lactic acidosis and one with an equal fall in pH from diarrhea (hyperchloremic acidosis): which has the larger rise in serum potassium from the shift alone?
blocks.explain: The patient with diarrhea-associated mineral acidosis. Chloride cannot follow H+ into cells, so K+ must leave; lactate enters cells with H+, so less K+ is displaced.

sections.title: Erythropoietin, the anemia of CKD, and secondary polycythemia

blocks.text: In adults about 90% of erythropoietin (EPO) is made by fibroblast-like peritubular interstitial cells in the renal cortex and outer medulla; most of the rest comes from the liver, which is the main source in the fetus. The kidney is a good oxygen sensor because its oxygen consumption is tied to sodium reabsorption, which tracks GFR and renal blood flow. Local tissue PO2 therefore reflects oxygen delivery (hemoglobin concentration times saturation times flow) rather than blood flow alone, so anemia and hypoxemia both raise EPO, while a fall in renal blood flow alone has relatively little effect.

blocks.title: Hypoxia to red cell production
steps: Oxygen delivery to renal interstitial cells falls
Prolyl hydroxylases lack O2 and stop hydroxylating HIF-alpha
VHL cannot tag HIF-alpha for proteasomal degradation
HIF-alpha pairs with HIF-beta and activates the EPO gene
EPO binds receptors on erythroid progenitors; JAK2 signaling
Progenitors survive and proliferate; reticulocytes rise in days
Oxygen delivery recovers and EPO falls
blocks.caption: Oxygen-dependent prolyl hydroxylation is the sensor; HIF-2 alpha is the main isoform driving renal EPO.

blocks.text: The prolyl hydroxylases need oxygen, iron, and 2-oxoglutarate, which is why oxygen is the controlling variable. EPO acts mainly on CFU-E and proerythroblasts, where its receptor signals through JAK2 and STAT5 to prevent apoptosis and drive proliferation and differentiation. Without EPO, most committed progenitors die.
Anemia of chronic kidney disease

As CKD destroys renal interstitium, EPO-producing cells are lost or transformed into scar-forming myofibroblasts, so EPO stays inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. The result is a hypoproliferative, normocytic, normochromic anemia with a low reticulocyte count. It usually becomes significant as GFR falls below about 30 to 60 mL/min. Contributing factors include shortened red cell survival in uremia, iron restriction by hepcidin (raised by inflammation and reduced renal clearance), and blood loss. Iron deficiency superimposed on CKD can make the anemia microcytic.
Secondary polycythemia

Secondary polycythemia is a raised red cell mass driven by EPO. It is appropriate when tissue hypoxia is real (high altitude, chronic lung disease, cyanotic heart disease) and inappropriate when EPO is made without hypoxia. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is the key renal example: loss of VHL function stabilizes HIF even in normal oxygen, so the tumor can secrete EPO autonomously while arterial saturation is normal. Other renal causes are cysts and hydronephrosis, which compress tissue and cause local hypoxia.

blocks.title: Distinguishing causes of erythrocytosis
rows: Renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, hemangioblastoma
blocks.caption: EPO level and oxygen saturation together locate the cause.

sections.title: Ethylene glycol: from alcohol to acid, gaps, and crystals

blocks.text: Ethylene glycol, a sweet-tasting antifreeze solvent, is itself only mildly toxic, acting much like ethanol on the brain. Its danger lies in its metabolites. Hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase, using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, oxidizes it to glycolaldehyde, the first and rate-limiting step. Aldehyde dehydrogenase, also NAD+-dependent, then forms glycolic acid. Conversion of glycolic acid to glyoxylic acid is slow, so glycolate accumulates and is the main cause of the acidosis. Glyoxylate is oxidized to oxalic acid, or diverted to glycine (a pyridoxine-dependent transamination) and to other nontoxic products (a thiamine-dependent pathway).

blocks.title: Metabolism of ethylene glycol
steps: Ethylene glycol: intact alcohol, raises measured osmolality
Alcohol dehydrogenase with NAD+ forms glycolaldehyde
Aldehyde dehydrogenase with NAD+ forms glycolic acid
Glycolate accumulates: high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Glycolate to glyoxylate to oxalic acid
Oxalate binds calcium: hypocalcemia and calcium oxalate crystals
Crystals and toxic metabolites injure proximal tubules: acute kidney injury
blocks.caption: The parent alcohol causes the osmolal gap; its acid products cause the anion gap and the organ injury.

blocks.text: The NADH produced by both dehydrogenases raises the cytosolic NADH to NAD+ ratio, which shifts pyruvate toward lactate and adds a lactic component to the acidosis. Oxalate chelates ionized calcium, causing hypocalcemia that can prolong the QT interval and produce tetany, and it precipitates as calcium oxalate in the proximal tubule. Crystals and the direct toxicity of glycolaldehyde and glycolate damage tubular cells, causing acute tubular injury with oliguria. In urine, calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals are needle or prism shaped, and dihydrate crystals have an envelope shape; their absence does not exclude poisoning.
The two gaps and their time course

Calculated serum osmolality is 2 times Na+ plus glucose divided by 18 plus BUN divided by 2.8 (glucose and BUN in mg/dL). A measured value more than about 10 mOsm/kg above this signals an unmeasured osmole. The anion gap, Na+ minus the sum of Cl- and HCO3-, is normally about 8 to 12 mEq/L. Early after ingestion the intact alcohol produces an osmolal gap with little acidosis. Over hours, as it is converted to acids, the osmolal gap falls and the anion gap rises, so a late presentation may show a large anion gap with a nearly normal osmolal gap. Blocking alcohol dehydrogenase, either by the competitive substrate ethanol or by fomepizole, confirms the model: the osmolal gap persists, the acids do not form, and the parent compound is excreted unchanged.

blocks.title: Reading both gaps
blocks.text: A confused man has Na+ 138 mEq/L, Cl- 102 mEq/L, HCO3- 8 mEq/L, glucose 90 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL, and a measured osmolality of 316 mOsm/kg. Anion gap: 138 minus 110 is 28 mEq/L, a high anion gap acidosis. Calculated osmolality: 276 plus 5 plus 5 is 286, so the osmolal gap is 30 mOsm/kg. Both gaps together point to a toxic alcohol caught partway through metabolism. Ethylene glycol has a molecular weight of 62, so each 1 mOsm/kg of gap corresponds to about 6.2 mg/dL, about 186 mg/dL here if ethylene glycol is the only unmeasured osmole. Calcium oxalate crystals in the urine and a falling calcium would confirm it.

blocks.title: Toxic alcohols compared
rows: Calcium oxalate crystals, acute tubular injury, hypocalcemia
Optic nerve and retinal injury, putaminal necrosis
Osmolal gap and ketosis without acidosis
blocks.caption: All three are oxidized first by alcohol dehydrogenase and all raise the osmolal gap.

sections.title: Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria in nephrotic syndrome

blocks.text: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g/day (in adults), hypoalbuminemia (below about 3 g/dL), edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria. The lipid changes follow from heavy glomerular protein loss through two broad mechanisms: the liver makes more lipoprotein, and the body clears lipoprotein more slowly.

On the synthetic side, the liver responds to low plasma oncotic pressure and urinary protein loss by increasing synthesis of many proteins at once, including albumin and apolipoprotein B. Hepatic cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase activity) rises, and more VLDL is secreted, which is converted to LDL. Lipoprotein(a) also rises. On the catabolic side, lipoprotein lipase activity in capillary endothelium falls, so triglyceride-rich VLDL and chylomicron remnants are cleared slowly, and hepatic LDL receptor activity is reduced, so LDL is removed slowly. Urinary loss of lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) impairs maturation of HDL. The typical result is high total and LDL cholesterol, with triglycerides rising as albumin falls further; the severity of hyperlipidemia is roughly inversely related to serum albumin.

blocks.title: From proteinuria to lipiduria
steps: Heavy glomerular albumin loss lowers plasma albumin
Low oncotic pressure stimulates hepatic protein and apoB synthesis
More VLDL and LDL are secreted
Lipoprotein lipase and LDL receptor activity fall; clearance slows
Plasma cholesterol and LDL rise; triglycerides rise in severe cases
Lipoproteins cross the damaged filter into tubular fluid
Lipid-laden tubular cells and casts appear in urine
blocks.caption: Increased production and reduced clearance together raise plasma lipids; the leaky barrier carries them into urine.

blocks.text: Lipiduria under the microscope

Proximal tubule cells take up the filtered lipid and protein, become engorged, degenerate, and are shed. A shed tubular cell (or macrophage) packed with lipid droplets is an oval fat body. When such cells or free droplets are trapped in a uromodulin matrix in the tubule, they form a fatty cast. Minimal change disease was historically called lipoid nephrosis because of lipid in tubular cells.

Cholesteryl esters in these droplets are anisotropic, so under polarized light each droplet shows a bright Maltese cross pattern (birefringence). Triglycerides are isotropic and do not polarize, but stain orange-red with fat stains such as Sudan III or Oil Red O, so the two methods are complementary. Starch granules from glove powder also show a Maltese cross; they are an artifact, recognized by their irregular, faceted shape and their location outside cells and casts.

blocks.predict: A urine sediment from a patient with 5 g/day proteinuria shows refractile droplets that do not polarize. Does this exclude lipiduria?
blocks.explain: No. Triglyceride droplets are isotropic and do not form Maltese crosses; only cholesteryl esters do. A fat stain such as Sudan III or Oil Red O would reveal them.
blocks.check: The paragraph on polarized light and fat stains.

integration.text: Each topic in this chapter is a transport or enzyme step read through a lab value. Physiology supplies the rules: saturable carriers explain glucosuria and overflow proteinuria, the Nernst relationship explains the potassium ECG, and oxygen-dependent hydroxylation explains why erythropoietin tracks oxygen delivery. Biochemistry supplies the enzymes: 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule, alcohol dehydrogenase and its NAD+ requirement, and the lipoprotein enzymes whose activity falls in nephrotic syndrome. Pathology shows where these steps fail: diabetic nephropathy, myeloma kidney, Fanconi syndrome, CKD with secondary hyperparathyroidism and anemia, VHL-deficient renal cell carcinoma, and oxalate crystal injury.

Several findings depend on a second variable, so they must be read in context. Glucosuria depends on GFR as well as plasma glucose, serum potassium on acid-base status and insulin as well as total body stores, PTH on magnesium as well as calcium, and the two toxic alcohol gaps on the time since ingestion. Reference ranges differ slightly between laboratories, and ECG changes correlate only loosely with the potassium value, so the trend and the whole clinical picture carry more weight than a single number.

summary: Glucose is reclaimed by SGLT2 (about 90%) and SGLT1 with Na+, then exits by GLUT2; carriers saturate at a Tm of about 375 mg/min.
Glucosuria starts at about 200 mg/dL because of splay; unreabsorbed glucose causes an osmotic diuresis with polyuria and volume depletion.

Glomerular proteinuria is albumin through a damaged barrier, overflow proteinuria is excess small protein such as light chains, and tubular proteinuria is failed proximal reclamation of beta-2 microglobulin; the dipstick detects mainly albumin.
PTH and low phosphate stimulate, and FGF23 and high phosphate suppress, proximal tubule 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
CKD: high phosphate, low calcitriol, low or normal calcium, high PTH. Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low phosphate. Vitamin D deficiency: low phosphate, high PTH.
Severe hypomagnesemia suppresses PTH release and action, so hypocalcemia persists until magnesium is replaced.
Insulin, beta-2 stimulation, and alkalosis move K+ into cells; acidosis, lysis, insulin deficiency, and hyperosmolality move it out.
Hyperkalemia gives peaked T waves, then wide QRS and sine wave; hypokalemia gives flat T waves and U waves.
Hypoxia stabilizes HIF in renal interstitial cells to make EPO; CKD causes normocytic anemia with low EPO, and renal cell carcinoma can cause polycythemia with high EPO and normal saturation.

Ethylene glycol gives an early osmolal gap, a later high anion gap acidosis, oxalate crystals, and hypocalcemia; nephrotic lipiduria shows oval fat bodies and fatty casts with Maltese crosses from cholesteryl esters.

verify: Renal threshold for glucose (about 180 to 200 mg/dL) and Tm (about 320 to 375 mg/min) vary between sources; this chapter uses the Guyton and Hall values.
The 90% and 10% split between SGLT2 and SGLT1 is the common teaching figure; some sources give 80 to 90% for SGLT2.
Tubular proteinuria is quoted as below 1 g/day or below 2 g/day in different sources.
Reference ranges for calcium, phosphate, magnesium, anion gap, and the osmolal gap cutoff differ between laboratories and textbooks; confirm the ranges NABNE uses.

The mechanism by which hypomagnesemia suppresses PTH (enhanced calcium-sensing receptor signaling through disinhibited G alpha subunits) is drawn from research literature; confirm the depth NABNE expects.
Calcitriol in vitamin D deficiency may be low, normal, or high depending on PTH drive and substrate; confirm how NABNE frames this row.
The GFR at which anemia of CKD becomes significant (quoted from below 60 to below 30 mL/min) varies between sources.
The proportion of renal cell carcinomas with erythrocytosis is quoted only approximately in sources, so it is not stated here.
Some blood gas analyzers misread glycolate as lactate in ethylene glycol poisoning (a lactate gap); confirm whether NABNE tests this.

The role of PCSK9 and ANGPTL4 in reduced LDL receptor and lipoprotein lipase activity in nephrotic syndrome is supported by research literature but is not in all standard texts; this chapter describes the activity changes without naming them.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: k-ecg-spectrum (ECG strips across hypokalemia and hyperkalemia) and glucose-titration (filtered, reabsorbed, and excreted glucose versus plasma glucose with threshold, splay, and Tm).
